findings.title: Fill the frame with bright, close, tilted terrain instead of a small globe floating in black space
findings.evidence: Brightness was measured on 320x180 samples. Ep01 (47 frames, one every 20 s, ep01s/f_*.jpg; sheet /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/visual/ep01_all.jpg): mean brightness 45/255 and 63% near-black pixels. About 20 of 47 frames show the whole globe floating in space, about 30 of 47 sit on a black or navy background, and only about 3 of 47 (12:03, 12:43, 15:23) are close terrain or satellite views that fill the frame. Benchmark frames: Contour Atlas brightness 161 with 0.3% near-black; Ice Melt 118 / 0.1%; How Big Australia 80 / 0.2%; RealLifeLore 166 / 0.3%; Kurzgesagt 133 / 13%; Wendover 105 / 13%. In every one, the subject fills the whole frame. vidIQ watch of grkuCssX_hI: about 40% of the runtime is terrain and lake-floor 3D at roughly 45 degrees, in daylight, with a hazy horizon (frame grkuCssX_hI_hq3: drained Lake Michigan at a 3/4 angle, olive land, beige lake bed, blue pools). Thumbnails make the same point: RealLifeLore zkbgLhBmzGo, Nepal WiRLNEl-4bk, Zanclean Mg0DMsmg9WM and Antarctica TudM_lSW8WA all use a tilted close terrain view, never a distant ball.
findings.recommendation: Make close terrain the default camera. Whole-globe-in-space shots should be at most 10% of the runtime and at most 4 s each, used only for establishing shots and transitions. Default framing is alt 0.03-0.3 with tilt 40-60 degrees, sky and haze in the top 15-25% of the frame, and sun:'camera' so the image is bright. QC targets per film: mean brightness 90-140 and near-black pixels under 15%, checked with /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/visual/scripts/lum.py on 1 frame every 20 s. Build a three.js 'terrain stage' from the existing DEM builder: a sky gradient instead of starfield black, distance fog, soft shadows and ambient occlusion. Use 10-30x vertical exaggeration and say so once in the narration, so nothing is passed off as real scale. Navy and black become UI box colours, not frame backgrounds.

findings.title: Size every label and number for a phone screen (about 3x larger than ep01)
findings.evidence: Ep01 labels measured at full resolution: '...ANTARCTICA: OPPOSITE THE ARCTIC OCEAN' at 3:03 has a cap height of about 22 px (2% of the frame height). 'MILLION YEARS AGO · SIMPLIFIED' at 9:43 is about 16 px of grey on black, and the 'MODEL' pill at 14:23 is tiny (crops: ep01/crop_183.jpg, ep01/crop_583.jpg). vidIQ watch of grkuCssX_hI says title and fact banners take about 6-8% of the frame height and data counters about 12-15%, in heavy ALL-CAPS sans with white or yellow fill on a dark box or thick stroke, popping in with a 0.25 s overshoot. Frame grkuCssX_hI_hq3 confirms it: '-351 FT' fills about 11% of the frame height in a navy box. ZWZWjXTnyEQ shows the year stamps '1910' and '1973' as big yellow condensed numbers, top-right. Antarctica's labels (TudM_lSW8WA_hq2/hq3) are a dark box with a yellow left bar and bold white caps. Ep01 mobile retention was 14% versus 50%+ on computer and TV; on a phone, a 2% label is under 1 mm tall.
findings.recommendation: Hard rules for the engine: label cap height at least 54 px (5%), key numbers 110-160 px (10-15%), and no secondary grey line under 36 px. Remove any sub-line that only says 'simplified'; say it in the narration instead. Text is white or yellow #FFD23F on a solid navy box (#0B1D28 at 85%) or with a 4-6 px dark stroke. Keep it inside the central 80% of the frame, with at most one label and one number on screen. Add a phone-check render to QC: downscale to 640x360 and confirm every label is still readable.

findings.title: Show one persistent on-screen gauge for the changing variable, plus a numbered countdown
findings.evidence: grkuCssX_hI (vidIQ watch, sections 3 and 4): a 'WATER LEVEL' widget sits top-right in every visual mode, with a vertical ruler, a sliding tick and a negative counter (-3 FT ... -351 FT). The film is framed as '30 FACTS COUNTING DOWN' with 'FACT 30' tags bottom-left, and these anchors stay in the same position across terrain, diorama and photo shots. Red-and-white striped surveyor poles stand inside the 3D scenes to show local drops ('TOLEDO -7.7 FT', 'BUFFALO +10.68 FT', '16.68 FT APART'). ZWZWjXTnyEQ uses year stamps as the same kind of anchor. Ep01 had a million-years counter (9:23-10:23) but it was small and only appeared in one sequence.
findings.recommendation: Each episode gets a persistent overlay layer (layer 5 or above, the whole film) that tracks its one changing variable: water level, ice thickness, year, depth, distance or people. Place it in a fixed corner at 12-15% of the frame height, with tick sounds (tick_counter) as it moves and an impact sound on milestones. Add a new F.gauge(ctx, value, range, {unit}) next to F.counter. If the script has a list or chapter structure, show a numbered tag at each step ('7 OF 10', or the chapter number plus a 2-4 word title) as a visible progress bar. It tells phone viewers how far they are and keeps open loops running.

findings.title: Show change live on one camera: drain, flood, peel or grow, never as a cut between two states
findings.evidence: grkuCssX_hI (vidIQ watch, sections 5 and 9): the water planes drop live on screen. Shelves dry out, isolated pools stay in deep basins, and a cross-section block drops in step with the 3D surface. The opening gag at 0:01 is a giant drain plug pulled on a chain. Other examples: syCnXSCxrZE floods coastlines with a '+70 m' tag; TudM_lSW8WA peels the ice sheet back like a lid (thumbnail) and splits the screen between a real Alps photo and a 3D render of the hidden Gamburtsev range (hq2); Mg0DMsmg9WM shows the drained Mediterranean bed as a terrain slab. Ep01's only praised visual, the 3D antipode overlay at 2:40-3:05, used the same idea: something changed on screen while the camera stayed on the same view.
findings.recommendation: Write every chapter's main visual as 'same camera, the variable changes': a 4-8 s slow orbit while the water plane, sea level, ice or time slider moves, with the gauge ticking and a riser, rumble or drain sound. Engine work: a DEM terrain mesh plus a translucent water plane with a depth-tinted colour ramp (#7FE0E6 shallow to #1A6FA0 to #0B2E4F deep), a foam line at the shoreline, and a darker wet 'bathtub ring' band with contour terraces on exposed seabed. Add an optional cross-section block that cuts the terrain like a cake. Reuse the existing overlay and morph tools for the reveal moments.

findings.title: Show people and events in one diorama mode built on the same terrain and light, not in one-off stylised scenes
findings.evidence: Contour Atlas gives about 25% of its runtime to low-poly 3D dioramas (vidIQ watch, sections 3 and 8): a 1910 town, a lighthouse and a 1973 island with a dashed red boundary (ZWZWjXTnyEQ hq1-hq3), locks, a captain beside a shipwreck full of Christmas trees, and an orbit around the broken Edmund Fitzgerald. Each is paired with a real black-and-white photo shown as a white-bordered tilted inset card. Tragic beats switch to storm, dark sky and snow on the same scenes. Iwo Jima (hEsjPdO3YQM, 4.4M on 3.5K subs) shows people only through public-domain archival photos: a gold-framed print on a dark textured background with a typewriter-style date, and a serif title with a gold rule. Kurzgesagt (_y9JuojAIg0, pHJIhxZEoxg) uses 100% illustrated characters with mascot reactions. Earthyphus (AVJPAbG-RbQ) gets laughs from a globe-headed stick figure. In ep01, characters stood in dark navy voids (2:23, 10:03), and the criticised corridor at 7:35-7:50 was a one-off dark interior that matched nothing else in the film.
findings.recommendation: Add a 'diorama' mode for 20-30% of the runtime. CC0 low-poly characters (Quaternius/Kenney) stand directly on the same DEM terrain tile, under the same sun and sky, with tilt-shift blur to sell the miniature look. The human story then plays out on the map, and a camera push takes us from the map into the diorama and back, so the film keeps one visual language. All humour goes here as 2-4 s character reactions or physical gags like the drain plug. Weather and light carry the mood (storm and snow for tragedy). Archival photos appear only as tilted white-bordered cards (0.25 s overshoot, 3-4 s, while the 3D world keeps moving behind), never as a static full-screen portrait. Retire the dark void stages.

findings.title: Cutting rhythm: average shot about 3.5-4 s, longest hold about 6.5 s, and a hook that previews the payoff shots
findings.evidence: grkuCssX_hI (vidIQ watch, section 2): about 17 cuts in 0:00-1:00 (average shot length about 3.5 s), about 15 in 10:00-11:00 (about 4.0 s), about 14 in the last minute (about 4.2 s); the longest hold is about 6.5 s, on drone footage. Its hook (section 1): the first 33 s is a montage of the film's best images (drain plug at 0:01, Superior 700+ ft below sea level at 0:05, caribou lane at 0:08, shipwrecks at 0:16-0:25), and the first live drain with the gauge starts at 0:35. The weak spots it found were repeated high-altitude terrain flyovers and long holds on static geology block diagrams (18:30-19:05, 21:05-21:30).
findings.recommendation: Keep the ENGINE cadence rules (an event every 2-3 s in minute 1, every 3-5 s after). Add hard limits: an average of 4 s or less between hard cuts or mode changes, no hold over 7 s, and a change of visual mode (terrain, diorama, photo card, cross-section, gauge close-up) at least every 20-40 s so no single mode runs long. The hook shows 3-5 of the film's best moving shots in the first 30 s under one narrated story question. That is a preview you see, not a spoken table of contents, which is what the ep01 critique objected to. No static block diagram on screen for more than 5 s.

findings.title: Show scale with familiar objects placed into the 3D scene
findings.evidence: grkuCssX_hI (vidIQ watch, section 9): the Statue of Liberty and the Gateway Arch are placed beside underwater cliffs, and striped surveyor poles stand in the water. a7mZgw86tXY (814K on 7.6K subs) is built on route lines and a drive-time chip ('12 hr 31 min / 1,009 km') laid over the map. RealLifeLore and Geoff thumbnails use a cut-out reveal and white curved arrows. The earlier benchmark's true-size overlays are already in the engine as moves.
findings.recommendation: Build a library of low-poly scale props: Statue of Liberty, Empire State Building, a 747, a school bus, a person, a blue whale. Drop them into the terrain at true scale, with a counter showing the height. Design our own neutral drive-time and distance chip (not a copy of any map app's interface) to anchor distances for US viewers. Keep the true-size drag over the USA as a recurring device.

findings.title: Colour and light: a daylight palette with weather for mood, and UI colour kept in boxes
findings.evidence: grkuCssX_hI (vidIQ watch, section 7): olive and sand land, cyan shallow water shading to navy in the deep, a bright sky with soft clouds, strong directional sun with soft ground shadows, golden-hour real footage, and storm or snow on tragic beats. The UI uses navy boxes, safety yellow, coral red and white throughout. Kurzgesagt uses saturated purple, teal and green with rim light. Iwo Jima uses a desaturated documentary grade with gold accents. Ep01 is mostly black and navy with an orange highlight (sample sheet), and its mean brightness of 45 is less than half that of any benchmark.
findings.recommendation: Revise the palette. The frame base is daylight terrain with sky gradient #9CC9E8 to #E8F1F6 and haze. Water uses the depth ramp in the 'show change live' finding. Hero orange #FF5A36 stays for highlights and red #E8412C for routes, boundaries and danger. Yellow #FFD23F is for numbers and years. Navy #0B1D28 appears only inside label and gauge boxes. Mood comes from light and weather (dusk, storm, snow), not from black backgrounds. Apply one shared grade lookup table to the terrain, diorama and photo-card modes so they read as one film.

findings.title: Real-world anchor shots for 10-15% of the runtime (public domain, no paid stock)
findings.evidence: About 20% of grkuCssX_hI is real drone footage, used at 0:00 and as breathers between facts. xiCwRsBn6mQ (2.6M) mixes Google Earth 3D with underwater and ship footage. RealLifeLore zkbgLhBmzGo and Wendover gLkbK8h_9fc and vIGub9r4a2o (frames hq1-hq3) anchor every map claim with a real photo of the place or its people. Iwo Jima uses public-domain US military photos.
findings.recommendation: Put each real place on screen within the first 1-2 s it is mentioned. Use public-domain moving footage (NOAA Ocean Exploration ROV, USGS, NASA ISS Earth views, US-government DVIDS) graded with the shared lookup table, or our own photoreal low flyover with a NASA GIBS high-resolution patch as a 'drone' shot. Keep it to 10-15% of the runtime and at most 5 s per clip. Label it only with the place name: no credits on screen, credits go in the description.

findings.title: Design the main visual so a frame from the film can be the thumbnail
findings.evidence: In the outliers, the thumbnail hero image is a stronger version of a shot that is actually in the film. Contour Atlas thumbnails show the drained basin seen at -351 FT in hq3. Mg0DMsmg9WM shows the drained Med slab. TudM_lSW8WA shows the ice lid peeled back. RealLifeLore zkbgLhBmzGo shows a globe cut-out. Iwo Jima shows an X-ray cutaway of the island with cyan tunnels. Ep01 has no frame like that: every sample is a distant globe.
findings.recommendation: Plan one hero shot per episode (tilted close terrain, one bold reveal, one highlight colour) and render a 4K still of it. That makes the thumbnail honest ('nothing fake presented as real') and gives the packaging team a strong base image.

keep: The 3D antipode overlay technique (ep01 2:40-3:05, praised by YouTube): a live overlay on a fixed camera. Make it the template for every main shot.

The photoreal globe stack (Blue Marble with bathymetry, DEM relief, atmosphere, night lights) and NASA GIBS high-resolution patches. Use them for establishing shots, transitions and 'drone' flyovers (at most 10% as a distant globe).
Hero-orange highlight with glow and a crisp white outline, great-circle arcs and true-size moves. They match RealLifeLore and Geography By Geoff and read well on phones if the camera is close.

F.counter rolling numbers timed to the spoken word, and the cadence rules in ENGINE.md (an event every 2-3 s in minute 1, every 3-5 s after). The Contour Atlas average shot length of 3.5-4.2 s confirms them.
The paleo-reconstruction 'time slider' idea (ep01 9:23-10:23): the variable changes on a fixed camera. It just needs a closer camera, bigger numbers and a persistent gauge.

The CC0 low-poly characters (Quaternius/Kenney) and the funny 3D gags (e.g. the classroom at 6:23). Contour Atlas proves low-poly reads as premium when it shares the world's light. Move the characters onto the terrain.
No burned-in subtitles in long-form. None of the long-form winners checked use full subtitles (the only caption pill seen was a small one in syCnXSCxrZE).
The sound-cue library tied to visual devices (whoosh on flights, ticks under counters, impact on reveals), plus new drain and rumble sounds for the water-plane reveals.
Word-timed scene scheduling from ElevenLabs timings, and the headless three.js plus Canvas2D engine on a Colab L4. The new terrain and diorama stages fit this pipeline.

findings.title: 1. The subject is too small on a phone: a small globe in a black frame for about three quarters of the film
findings.evidence: Whole film measured at 5 fps, 96x54 px: in 74.0% of frames at least 45% of the frame is near-black (luma below 18/255). Only 7.1% of the runtime is full-bleed (under 15% black). In the first 131 s, which is the mobile average view duration of 2:11, the figure is 79.4%. At phone size the globe is a disc about 190 px wide inside 390 px of black. Frames: audit/phone/t00m00.0s.jpg, t00m20.0s.jpg, t00m40.0s.jpg, t13m40.0s.jpg; the whole 13:27-14:17 run (sheets/phone_x1330_1416_longdark.jpg). For comparison, the full-bleed tilted shots at 7:50, 12:20, 12:40 and 15:08-15:14 read perfectly at 390 px (sheets/curated_phone_premium.jpg). Metric script: research/visual/audit_scripts/metrics.py; arrays m_black.npy and m_lum.npy.
findings.recommendation: Make the tilted full-bleed satellite/terrain camera the default look for ep02, at 60% of runtime or more (alt 0.12-0.5, tilt 35-55 deg, horizon and atmosphere visible). The subject should fill at least 60-70% of the frame. Use whole-globe-on-black only for 2-4 s establishing shots and transitions. When the globe is used, fill frame height or more (crop the limb) rather than show a centred 50%-width disc.

findings.title: 2. All labels, captions and legends are sized for a TV and come out about 1 mm tall on a phone
findings.evidence: Measured on native 1080p crops (audit/crops/label_ruler_native.jpg): pills and captions use Barlow at about 26-35 px cap height (2.5-3% of frame height), which is 5-7 px at 390 px wide. Several are grey-on-black. Examples: 0:20 'TWO-THIRDS OF ALL LAND'; 0:25 'NEARLY 9 IN 10 OF US' (grey, about 30 px, so about 6 px on a phone; crops/t00m25.0s_crop2.jpg); the 1:18-1:24 quote pill; 2:20 'NORTH POLE'; the 3:02.5 caption 'MOST OF ANTARCTICA: OPPOSITE THE ARCTIC OCEAN'; the 3:12 colour legend (about 3 px on a phone, and it carries the meaning of the 4:00-4:40 map); 10:00 'MILLION YEARS AGO - SIMPLIFIED' (crops/t10m00.0s_crop.jpg); 5:20 'THE NORMAL FORM OF A CONTINENT', a near-transparent pill on pink that cannot be read even at 1080p (crops/t05m20.0s_crop2.jpg); 15:11 'A CONTINENT CRACKING IN A Y'. Only the Bebas headlines survive, at about 55-70 px cap: 0:33, 2:42.5, 3:16, 5:08, 7:42.5, 14:56.
findings.recommendation: Set a new phone floor. Any text the viewer must read gets at least 64 px cap height (6% of frame height), and headlines get 110-150 px. Use #F4F6FA on an 80% dark plate, never grey secondary text for key facts, at most 4 words and at most one text element at a time. Replace legends with colour-coded headline words, as in the 2:42.5 'OCEAN ON TOP. LAND AT BOTTOM.' Before approval, QC every text frame at 390 px. The style-guide rule of '30-38 px labels' in bench_visual.md must be retired.

findings.title: 3. About 50 s of static paper and portraits sits right where mobile viewers leave (0:57-1:16 and 1:40-2:12)
findings.evidence: Mobile average view duration is 2:11. Inside that window: the 1655 sepia map and the Bacon title page, portrait and three Latin text plates from 0:57 to 1:16 (sheets/phone_r0030_0130_hook_bacon_1.jpg, _2.jpg). Then the Humboldt portrait, a dense book page, and five frames of mock cream 'papers' with grey dash bars from 1:40 to 2:12 (sheets/phone_x0133_0239_mobile_dropzone_1.jpg; frames audit/full/t01m51.0s.jpg, t02m06.0s.jpg, t02m09.0s.jpg). That is about 44% of the first 131 s spent on beige stills over a dark textured backdrop, with Latin and body text that cannot be read at phone size.
findings.recommendation: In the first 3 minutes, allow no more than 3 s per archival still and never two in a row. Keep the camera moving on the Earth and bring history into the map: put the quote as one big pill on the coastline it describes, or flash the portrait as a small badge over the place. No page text smaller than about 5 words per frame. Cut mock documents entirely.

findings.title: 4. Style whiplash: at least 12 visual languages in 15 minutes
findings.evidence: Counted on the 20-s grid (sheets/full_grid20s_1-3.jpg): photoreal globe (about 42% of samples), flat satellite world map (0:10, 3:40-4:40), archival scans (1:00, 5:20, 6:00, 8:20, 9:00), mock grey-bar papers (1:51-2:09, 11:40), low-poly Quaternius adventurer (2:21-2:36, 3:32, 5:25-5:53, 7:37-7:43, 14:10), Kenney blocky kids (6:20), flat-vector grey corridor (7:45-7:48), flat cartoon cutaway Earth (0:42, 2:57, 3:28, 6:40, 14:40), cream/orange/navy paleo globe (9:20-10:20), cream polar discs (2:40), pinboard (7:00), stylised 3D zebra seafloor (8:40), teardrop pins (11:00-11:20), and a film-strip recap (14:59-15:05). The corridor at 7:35-7:50 that YouTube criticised is only the worst case: sheets/phone_r0730_0755_corridor.jpg.
findings.recommendation: Use one visual world for ep02: the photoreal Earth (globe plus tilted DEM terrain and seafloor). Every graphic should be an overlay that lives on that Earth, lit by the same sun. Do funny scenes inside that world: comic camera moves, map objects with physical behaviour, and a properly lit hero prop or character standing on real terrain. Drop the Kenney blocky set, flat-vector interiors, pinboards and flat cartoon cutaways. If a cross-section is needed, cut into the real DEM terrain block.

findings.title: 5. The low-poly characters and props look like a game blockout and are too small for gags to read
findings.evidence: 2:21-2:24 'Santa's houseboat': box house, cylinder pole and octagonal slab floe, all flat-lit (audit/full/t02m21.0s.jpg). The line is funny and the image is not. 7:37-7:43: a faceted adventurer in an empty blue or purple gradient void, with two disagreeing shadows and a quote card half-covering a globe (audit/full/t07m42.5s.jpg). 5:25-5:53: the character is about 10% of frame height, about 20 px on a phone (sheets/phone_x0525_0557_longhold.jpg). 6:20: three Kenney block kids seen from behind, with blurred grey 'chalk' placeholder lines (audit/full/t06m20.0s.jpg). The faces have no readable expression, so the comedy depends entirely on the VO.
findings.recommendation: If characters stay, use one rig only, at higher fidelity. Each gag shot gets the character at 40% of frame height or more, standing on real DEM ice or terrain with the globe's sun, atmosphere, contact shadow, AO and rim light, plus shallow depth of field. Animate with anticipation and overshoot and keep each gag to 2-4 s. Otherwise build humour from map-native motion design (objects sliding, whip-pans, true-size drags with impact SFX) instead of characters in voids.

findings.title: 6. Murky, underexposed frames that disappear on a phone at auto-brightness
findings.evidence: Mean luma of the film is about 40/255 (per-minute means range 17.7-67.7; minute 13 is the darkest at 17.7). 0:54 is a 4-split of almost-black globes (audit/full/t00m54.0s.jpg). 4:50-5:06 is a dark globe on a sepia background with ghosted engraved globes (sheets/phone_r0450_0510_subscard.jpg). 7:35 is a dark book over a near-invisible globe. 13:27-14:17 is 50 s continuously below luma 28. There are 40 or more segments of 2 s or longer below luma 28 (metrics.py output).
findings.recommendation: Raise the globe exposure by 0.5-1 stop and keep the lit hemisphere toward the camera (sun:'camera'). Never show a night-side globe unless the city lights are the point. Replace pure-black space with a deep navy gradient. Target an average frame luma of about 70-110. Never stack ghosted texture backgrounds behind a dark subject. No split screens of 4.

findings.title: 7. Rendering defects that read as bugs at phone size
findings.evidence: 0:00, the very first frame: a grey specular smudge on the Pacific beside the highlighted South America (crops/globe_specular_smudge_0000_1340.jpg). 1:18-1:24: Antarctica rendered as an overexposed white blob with bubbly cloud sprites (audit/full/t01m21.0s.jpg). 10:00: a dark blurred smudge behind the '115' counter, sitting on the orange continent (crops/t10m00.0s_crop.jpg). 12:00: highlight fills cut by straight rectangle edges inside the tiles (audit/full/t12m00.0s.jpg). 5:08: the chapter headline is laid over title-page text. 15:05: an empty film-strip slot with a stray red dot.
findings.recommendation: Add a phone-scale QC gate: render every shot's middle frame at 390x219 and reject smudges, blown whites, clipped fills, and text over text. Tame the camera-sun specular (lower intensity, broader lobe). No additive blob sprites over the globe. Readability plates must be crisp rounded rectangles, never blurred dark smears.

findings.title: 8. Placeholder graphics, an on-screen citation, and mock documents that break the owner's rules
findings.evidence: Grey dash 'text' on mock papers at 1:51-2:09 and 11:40, and blurred grey chalk lines at 6:20: they look like unfinished wireframes. 11:40 shows 'DIETZ & HOLDEN (1970)', an author-year citation on screen (audit/full/t11m40.0s.jpg), which violates 'no on-screen sources/citations'. 2:06-2:09 shows a '1976' mock paper titled 'THE DRIP, REVISITED' built from fake text bars, so it looks like a real publication that it is not (risk under 'nothing fake presented as real').
findings.recommendation: No mock documents in ep02. Either show a real public-domain scan cropped to 3-5 big words, or tell the moment on the map. Never show author names or years as a reference. Keep sources in the description only.

findings.title: 9. CTA graphics break the story mid-film and hold the end too long
findings.evidence: 5:00-5:07: a 'JUICE CHECK ?' sign flies around while a red SUBSCRIBE pill with a red glow lands over the tetrahedron reveal (audit/full/t05m04.0s.jpg, t05m06.0s.jpg). At the end, the 'WATCH NEXT' box and SUBSCRIBE appear at about 15:15-15:17 while the VO runs to 15:21.7. After that comes about 12 s of near-static hold with an empty box. The last detected cut is 15:14.0, leaving a 19.8 s uncut stretch to 15:33.8 (sheets/phone_r1450_1534_ending.jpg).
findings.recommendation: No subscribe graphic or ask before the final 20 s. Start the end-screen layout only when the last VO word ends. Keep the background moving (slow push along the Afar rift) and limit the end hold to 10-12 s. Keep 'Juice Check' purely as a verdict stamp.

findings.title: 10. Data maps and grids that need a legend or hold too many items to read on a phone
findings.evidence: 4:00-4:40: a cyan/yellow antipode world map whose meaning rests on the 3 px legend at 3:12 (audit/phone/t04m00.0s.jpg). 3:40-3:52: a flat dark map with small shapes and a 1 px equator line. 11:00-11:20: translucent teardrop pins overlap and hide the map (audit/full/t11m20.0s.jpg). 12:00: 8 thumbnails of about 180x120 px (about 36x24 px on a phone) plus 4 tiles, with the bottom 40% of the frame empty (audit/full/t12m00.0s.jpg).
findings.recommendation: One idea per frame with 1-2 highlighted shapes at most. Show lists as a sequence of full-frame tilted shots joined by whip-pans, about 1-1.5 s each, never as grids. State colour meaning in the headline's coloured words. Keep the base map visible under highlights: relief shows through and the outline is crisp white.

findings.title: 11. The same composition repeats for long stretches: centred globe, same size, same side
findings.evidence: Longest uncut stretches (detected at 5 fps): 5:24.6-5:56.8 (32.2 s, tetrahedron plus checklist panel), 2:59.0-3:24.8 (25.8 s), 4:48.2-5:06.6 (18.4 s), 4:04.8-4:21.0 (16.2 s), 8:34.2-8:49.8 (15.6 s), 11:46.8-12:02.0 (15.2 s), 3:38.0-3:53.0 (15.0 s). 13:27-14:17 has cuts, but each new shot is again a centred globe of the same size with a thin arrow (sheets/phone_x1330_1416_longdark.jpg). Average spacing between detected cuts is 5.3 s, which is on benchmark. The problem is sameness of scale and framing, not cut count.
findings.recommendation: Rotate shot scale every 5-7 s (wide establishing, then tilted regional, then close detail or terrain) and alternate the subject between the left and right thirds. Cap any one composition at 8 s. On the phone, a change of scale reads as an event even when the cut rate stays the same.

findings.title: 12. Lines and arrows are too thin to read on a phone
findings.evidence: Meaningful strokes are about 3-5 px at 1080p, about 1 px on a phone: the 0:05 great-circle arc, the 13:30-14:00 yellow drift arrows (audit/phone/t13m40.0s.jpg), the 3:40 equator line, the 3:00 red/cyan outlines, and the 0:25 hemisphere ring.
findings.recommendation: Draw meaningful lines at 8-12 px at 1080p with a dark 4 px under-stroke and glow. Arrowheads should be at least 40 px. Animate the line drawing on, with a moving head dot, so the eye finds it.

keep: The photoreal globe base, and above all the antipode device at 2:47-3:05: the shape lifts off, flies to the far side of the globe, and a colour-coded overlap is revealed. YouTube praised it, and it still reads at 390 px (audit/phone/t02m50.0s.jpg, t03m05.0s.jpg).

Tilted, full-bleed satellite and bathymetry shots: 7:50 Europe with Austria, 12:20 Florida, 12:40 South Africa, and 15:08-15:14 the Afar 'Y' with a glowing rift line. These are the most premium frames in the film and the best on a phone. Make this the default camera for ep02.

One saturated hero-orange highlight on real imagery (0:00 South America, 0:40 USA, 3:20 China, 12:20 Florida, 7:50 Austria): a single readable focus at phone size. Let the relief show through slightly and add a crisp white outline.

Big Bebas two-colour headlines that state the idea in at most 5 words: 0:33 'WHY DO THE CONTINENTS POINT SOUTH?', 2:42.5 'OCEAN ON TOP. LAND AT BOTTOM.', 3:16 'DIG STRAIGHT DOWN TO CHINA?', 14:56 'NOT AN ACCIDENT. A BREAKUP.'. These are the only text that survives at phone size.
The 'Juice Check' verdict stamp as a brand device (1:30 'JUICE CHECK: FALSE', 13:00 'IT'S COMPLICATED'). It is big and readable. Use it for verdicts only, never as a subscribe ask.
Real archival photos shown big and briefly (8:20 the 1930 Greenland photo filling the frame, 9:00 Wegener): authentic and emotional. Keep them full-bleed and at most 3 s.

The idea behind the depth and cross-section gag at 2:27-2:36 (standing on the ice with a ruler down to the seafloor, number on the spoken word). It reads on a phone; rebuild it on real DEM terrain and seafloor instead of a flat 2D profile.
Funny VO lines such as 'Santa's workshop is technically a houseboat' and 'utter, damned rot'. The writing carries the humour; the visuals need to match its quality.
Overall cut rhythm of about 5.3 s average between detected cuts, which matches the benchmark.

findings.title: 1. Phone-first typography: ep01's 30-38 px labels can't be read on a phone held upright; set a 56-64 px minimum and draw text after post-processing
findings.evidence: ENGINE.md sets labels at 30-38 px. In ep01 at 2:00 the 'TWO-THIRDS OF ALL LAND' label is about 36 px (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/ep01/t0020.jpg). In an upright phone the 16:9 player is about 393 pt wide, a 0.205x scale, so a 36 px label shows at about 7 pt. The simulation sheet /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/proto_phone_sim.jpg shows the 32-36 px labels can't be read, the 62 px pill (Barlow Condensed 800, 80% plate, hero-orange border) can, and the 128 px depth counter reads at a glance. This matches ep01's data: mobile viewers averaged 2:11 (14%), computer and TV viewers 50%+.
findings.recommendation: Add presets to fx.js: F.label (minimum 56-64 px, Barlow Condensed 800, tracking 0.04, rgba(6,9,15,0.8) plate, 2-3 px accent border, 3 px leader and r=9 dot), F.kicker (44 px) and big numbers at 140-220 px. Keep labels to 3-4 words, at most 2 text items on screen, and inside the top two-thirds of the frame (mobile player controls sit at the bottom). Draw all text on a separate UI layer after the world post-process so bloom and grain never soften it. Have still.cjs QA log the smallest text size used per frame and fail anything under 52 px. Effort 3-4 h. Risk low. Render cost about zero locally and on the GPU (text sprites are cached). Visual gain: high for 44% of viewers.

findings.title: 2. New shot type: real 3D terrain and seafloor from elevation data with a lowering water plane ('drain the sea'); prototype done, data path verified
findings.evidence: Prototype page /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/www/scout_drain.html; stills in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/proto_drain_sequence.jpg (Strait of Gibraltar at 0, -300 and -1200 m). Data: NOAA ETOPO 2022 at 15 arc-seconds (about 450 m) through THREDDS WCS returns float GeoTIFF subsets in one request (a 6 by 3.3 degree box was 4.6 MB). This works now: www.ngdc.noaa.gov/thredds/wcs/global/ETOPO2022/15s/15s_surface_elev_netcdf/ETOPO_2022_v1_15s_N45W015_surface.nc?service=WCS&version=1.0.0&request=GetCoverage&coverage=z&bbox=...&format=GeoTIFF_Float. dem.py's AWS Terrarium tiles are reachable too, but their seafloor is coarser (mostly ETOPO1 grade, my assessment). Mesh: 720x396 grid (570k triangles), a 500 m GIBS Blue Marble drape on land, a depth colour ramp on the seafloor, and a water shader tinted by depth with a shoreline foam line. Local cost 1.85 s/frame (MSAA, 4k shadow map) against 0.37 s for the base globe; trivial on the L4. The prototype also exposed a factual trap: at -300 m my 'LAND BRIDGE' label is false in the data, because a channel through the strait is still open (frame /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/dl/st_drain/f000001.jpg). Other flaws: the mesh's flat edge shows at the horizon (top right), and 6x vertical exaggeration makes mountains spiky.
findings.recommendation: Build lib/terrain.js (10-14 h). It covers: an ETOPO WCS fetch tool writing h16 PNG plus metadata, mesh LOD, the land drape (GIBS 500 m or 31 m HLS) with a seafloor ramp, the water shader, sky and fog, a camera keyed in lat/lon/alt, project() for labels, and a globe-to-terrain hand-off (a match-cut at the same lat/lon/heading with a short fade). Add a connectivity check (flood-fill from a seed in each basin at level L) so any 'land bridge', 'lake' or 'island' claim matches the data. Cap vertical exaggeration at 2-3x and note it in the description. Fade to fog before the mesh edge, or add a wider low-resolution skirt. Risk medium (the hand-off seam, curvature on large areas). Render cost: about 1.9 s/frame locally (fine for previews), negligible on the GPU. Visual gain: very high. It is the native format of the 'We Drained X' breakouts listed in the context.

findings.title: 3. One finishing pipeline: 2x supersampling, then a WebGL post pass on the world layer (bloom, colour grade or LUT, slight chromatic aberration, vignette, grain), with text drawn on top
findings.evidence: globe.js creates its renderer with antialias:false and pixel ratio 1, so the limb, outlines and overlay edges alias. fx.post() does vignette and grain in Canvas2D (slow on software rendering, and it never touches the 3D stages consistently). The r170 postprocessing/, shaders/ and objects/ (Sky, Water, Lensflare) are in node_modules/three/examples/jsm but NOT in www/jsm, which only has libs/loaders/utils; copying them (about 0.7 MB) is enough, since they load through film.html's import map (checked with /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/www/caps.html). LUTPass, LUTCubeLoader, SMAAPass, SSAARenderPass and OutputPass are all present. Local measurements (SwiftShader, 4 cores, 10-frame runs): base 0.37 s/frame; base + 2x SSAA 0.59 s; full upgrade at 1x 0.94 s; full upgrade at 2x 2.1 s. On the L4, ep01 ran at 450 frames in 32 s (about 71 ms/frame, mostly JPEG encoding and transfer), so expect about +20-40%. SwiftShader caps found: 8192 max texture, 4x MSAA, float render targets OK. Before/after: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/proto_globe_compare.jpg (top-right panel; clipped cloud highlights show the grade needs a highlight shoulder).
findings.recommendation: Split every frame into a WORLD layer (globe, stages, terrain, photos), then a single post pass (shared LUT .cube with teal shadows and warm highlights, bloom threshold about 0.8, a filmic highlight shoulder, edge-only chromatic aberration of 1-2 px, vignette about 0.3, animated grain about 0.035), then a UI layer drawn crisp on top. Running globe, characters, terrain and photos through the same grade gives one visual language, which answers YouTube's 'corridor scene clashed' critique. Add a draft flag in Q that turns off SSAA and post for local previews. Effort 6-8 h. Risk low-medium: an 8 MB texture upload per frame, interaction with the fade layer (layerA), and bloom must never touch text. Visual gain: medium-high on every frame.

findings.title: 4. Cloud layer with cast shadows for wide and establishing shots, built from public-domain NASA GIBS imagery (the NASA download site is unreachable here)
findings.evidence: eoimages.gsfc.nasa.gov, home of the classic Blue Marble cloud_combined_8192 and the 21600 px world.topo.bathy, is unreachable from this environment (connection reset at the proxy; logged in recentRelayFailures). GIBS works. I built a cloud mask from MODIS Terra+Aqua true colour on 2025-03-21 minus cloud-free Blue Marble NG (scripts: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/scripts/gibs_level.py, cloudmask.py; preview: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/proto_cloudmask_preview.jpg). It shows real cyclones and fronts. Flaws: straight seams where satellite passes from different hours meet (visible in the North Atlantic in the proto_globe_compare top-right panel) and Arctic sea ice counted as cloud. At alt 0.30 the 4k cloud layer looked blocky and smeared (first version of the oblique render, since superseded). Rendering: a cloud sphere at r=1.007 plus shadows computed in the existing earth shader by a runtime string patch, so no new pass is needed. Local cost is part of the 0.94 s/frame upgrade at 1x; negligible on the GPU.
findings.recommendation: Use VIIRS NOAA-20 or SNPP CorrectedReflectance_TrueColor instead. Its wider passes leave no equatorial gaps, so seams are fewer and smaller. Take one date near an equinox (both poles lit), mosaic at GIBS level 4-5 (10-20k px; GPU only, since three.js downscales automatically to 8192 on SwiftShader for previews), mask out sea ice and ice sheets with a Blue Marble whiteness test, and keep the alpha gamma about 1.7 so thin cloud stays thin. Rules: fade clouds out below alt about 0.6 unless a regional 250 m cloud crop is loaded; dim clouds to 30% whenever a highlight overlay is active (the map story comes first); allow a slow cloud drift of 0.02-0.05 deg/s for life. Effort 5-7 h. Risk medium (seams, readability of highlights). Visual gain: large realism jump on the opening and establishing shots, the frames that matter most for the first 30 s.

findings.title: 5. Motion blur by averaging several sub-frames, used only on fast moves; render time on the GPU makes this affordable
findings.evidence: film.html's renderFrame(f) is a pure function of t = f/FPS, and scenes draw deterministically from local time, so sub-frame sampling fits the engine's contract. The ep01 benchmark asked for whip blur but the engine has no such pass (r170 AfterimagePass is a trail effect, not motion blur). GPU budget: the ep01 film took about 15 min on the L4 with about 71 ms/frame, dominated by encoding. Blurring the roughly 15% of frames with fast camera, arc or move motion at N=6 should raise the total to about 1.3x, or about 20 min (estimate). Locally it is prohibitive (N times the 0.4-2 s frame cost), so previews stay at N=1. Caveat: shots that redraw overlay canvases every frame (ep01's paleo refreshOverlay) pay N times their Canvas2D and upload cost.
findings.recommendation: Add an accumulation path: for frames flagged by a per-scene blur(lt) hint, or by an automatic camera-speed check in camAt (heading, lat/lon and log-alt rate), render N=6-8 sub-frames over a 180-degree shutter into a float WebGL target and average them before the UI layer. Text stays sharp because it is drawn after. Effort 4-5 h. Risk low-medium (scenes that are not strictly time-pure). Visual gain: removes strobing on whip pans and space-to-place zooms, a cinematic cue viewers read as 'expensive'.

findings.title: 6. Sharper close-ups: more regional patch slots with cross-fades, GIBS 500 m and 31 m imagery, and the 8k normal map that sits unused on disk
findings.evidence: The base map is day_8k.jpg (8192x4096, about 4.9 km/px) and goes soft below alt about 0.5 (proto_globe_compare bottom-left). globe.js supports only ONE patch at a time (patchOn), so zooms pop between patches. GIBS checks: BlueMarble_ShadedRelief_Bathymetry and NextGeneration are served on the 500m tile set (top level 7 works, level 8 returns 400); HLS_S30, Landsat_WELD (true colour) and ASTER_GDEM shaded relief are on the 31.25m set. A level-7 patch for Iberia and Morocco (4551x3640, 3.1 MB) visibly sharpens the Atlas and Rif in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/dl/st_up1p/f000001.jpg. tex/normal_8k.png (39 MB) and tex/hgt_8k.png (47 MB) exist but ep01 never references them; Globe.init defaults to normal_4k. The bathymetry relief normals give the seafloor a lumpy look at oblique angles (bottom panels).
findings.recommendation: Give the globe shader 2-3 patch slots with independent alpha so a 500 m patch can cross-fade into a 31 m patch during a zoom, each with a matching regional normal map from dem.py or ETOPO. For GPU finals, load normal_8k and an optional 16384x8192 GIBS level-5 base (local SwiftShader auto-downsizes to its 8192 limit). Halve the relief strength over water. Effort 3-5 h. Risk low. Render cost: a one-off texture upload per shot, negligible per frame. Visual gain: medium, only on shots below alt 0.5.

findings.title: 7. Ocean sun glint: worth it (1-2 h). Physically based atmosphere: not worth it for ep02
findings.evidence: The current shader has a single broad specular lobe, which reads as a plastic sheen across the North Atlantic (proto_globe_compare top-left). I prototyped a multi-lobe glint that brightens toward grazing angles, plus a 16x6-sample ray-marched sky scattering shell (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/www/scout_globe.html). The atmosphere took the most local time (oblique shot 3.0 s/frame), first overexposed badly (the intensity must match the display-space lighting), and after retuning gave a less blue, less attractive horizon than the existing cheap rim (compare the bottom panels). On the GPU the cost is negligible; the problem is tuning time.
findings.recommendation: Ship the multi-lobe glint with sun:'world' on ocean shots, so a sharp sun hotspot plus a soft halo sits on the water (1-2 h, no measurable cost). Keep the existing analytic atmosphere. Add only a warm terminator and sunset band plus a light blue haze toward the horizon on tilted shots (2 h). Postpone a proper precomputed-scattering atmosphere (6-10 h) until after ep02.

findings.title: 8. Funny scenes inside the real world: characters on the same terrain, lighting and grade instead of abstract stages
findings.evidence: YouTube's critique: the stylised corridor scene at 7:35-7:50 clashed with the photoreal globe. ep01 placed low-poly actors on flat blue gradient voids (contact sheet /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/ep01_sheet.jpg; the 7:40 and 8:20 frames). Models on disk: adventurer.glb, astronaut.glb, mini_male_a.glb. Reachable CC0 sources: three.js RobotExpressive.glb (464 KB on raw.githubusercontent; clips Wave/Yes/No/ThumbsUp/Dance/Jump/Death/Sitting; a ready mascot), Soldier.glb, quaternius.com. kenney.nl, github.com/KenneyNL and poly.pizza return 403 through the proxy. three r170 has MeshToonMaterial, OutlineEffect and ToonShader.
findings.recommendation: Stage gags on the terrain meshes from finding 2. Example: a giant character stepping across the dried strait, lit by the same sun with shadows, fog and LUT, plus a soft contact shadow and rim light, so jokes live in the documentary world. Keep scale gags obviously playful; nothing staged as real. Pick one recurring CC0 character with expressive clips for continuity across episodes. Effort 6-10 h after the terrain library exists. Risk medium (tone and readability). Visual gain: high for the owner's 'real animation, funny scenes' request, and it removes the style clash.

findings.title: 9. Framing for phones: fill the frame with the subject; whole-globe shots leave about half the phone frame black
findings.evidence: The phone simulation (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/ep02/engine_scout/proto_phone_sim.jpg) shows ep01's whole-globe shots at alt 2.5-3 as a small ball on black, with the highlighted country tiny. The tilted terrain frame fills 100% of the frame and reads instantly. ep01's praised antipode overlay worked because it was large, semi-transparent with a glow outline, and centred (ep01 frame at 2:55).
findings.recommendation: Add camera presets: 'establish' (alt 2.2, at most 3 s, opening and transitions only), 'region' (alt 0.8-1.4, tilt 25-40, lookOffset so the subject fills 50-70% of frame height) and 'ground' (terrain library, tilt 50-65). Make highlights semi-transparent fills with glow and a white outline (the praised antipode style) rather than flat opaque paint (the 2:00 frame shows the flat paint). Effort about 2 h (presets plus style-guide update). Risk low. No render cost.

findings.title: 10. Encoding: frames go through two lossy JPEG/x264 steps with 4:2:0 colour, and the ep01 master is 6.6 Mbps
findings.evidence: grabBlob uses canvas JPEG (my test frame decodes as 4:2:0 chroma), piped as mjpeg into x264 yuv420p. ffprobe of /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/deliver/ep01/video_final.mp4: High profile, 1920x1080, yuv420p, 6.59 Mbps. Saturated hero-orange outlines and thin red text lose colour resolution twice, and the grain asked for in finding 3 needs bitrate to survive YouTube's re-encode.
findings.recommendation: On the GPU, raise the frame JPEG quality to 0.98, or pipe raw RGBA where bandwidth allows. Master at CRF 14-16 and, as the earlier visual benchmark already recommends, upscale the final to 2560x1440 so YouTube serves its higher-bitrate VP9/AV1 encode. Effort 1-2 h. Risk low. GPU cost: slightly larger chunk files (keep disk limits in mind).

keep: Deterministic pure-function-of-time renderer (film.html renderFrame) with chunked, restart-safe Colab L4 rendering (15-20x faster than SwiftShader): every upgrade above plugs into it, and render time on the GPU is effectively free
The photoreal globe base (Blue Marble with bathymetry, VIIRS night lights, starfield, analytic atmosphere rim): the cheap rim looked better than my ray-marched scattering prototype, so keep it
The praised antipode overlay style (2:40-3:05): semi-transparent fill plus glow plus crisp white outline drawn in 2D over the globe. Make it the house highlight style and drop flat opaque fills
The geo toolkit: Natural Earth outlines projected crisply in Canvas2D, great-circle arcs, true-size moves, markers, label leaders
The regional patch mechanism (setPatch) and the tools dem.py (AWS Terrarium) and gibs.py (NASA GIBS); both data sources are reachable, and GIBS also serves 31.25 m HLS and Landsat layers
Cached text sprites in fx.js (cheap) and the local font set (Bebas Neue, Barlow Condensed 500/700/800, Inter 400-900, Anton, Oswald, Archivo Black, JetBrains Mono, Playfair)
The sound-cue system (api.cue) tied to visual events
The three r170 add-ons already in node_modules (postprocessing, shaders, Sky/Water/Lensflare, LUT and loaders); they only need copying into www/jsm, with no new dependency

result.built:
I built CineGlobe, a cinematic drop-in replacement for ep01's globe, plus a lab page that renders the same camera through the old engine (before) and the new one (after).

result.production_use:
How to adopt it (the steps are also in the header of cineglobe.js):
1. Move lab/globe/cineglobe.js to www/lib/ and clouds_8k.jpg to www/tex/, then fix the default `clouds` path in init().
2. In film.html, api.globe(): `globe = new CineGlobe(W, H, {ss: Q.draft ? 1 : 2}); await globe.init();`. A draft flag gives 1x previews.
3. In api.drawGlobe(ctx, state, look), pass the frame index so the grain moves: `ctx.drawImage(globe.render(Math.round(t*FPS)), 0, 0)`.
4. In edit.js, make `post` a no-op for this look. CineGlobe already applies vignette and grain to the world layer, and the old F.post would double them and darken the text.
5. Don't pass ep01's LOOK0. Its specAmt 0.5 and desat 0.12 were tuned for the old shader; pass only what a shot changes.

What does not change: globeShot keys, overlays (setOverlay / fillEquirect, and the antipode style), patches, project() for labels, arcs, moves, markers, and crossfades through layerA.

New camera-state keys:
- clouds 0..1 (0.6-0.8 for story shots).
- cloudOff, cloud drift in degrees (0.04*t).

I built a working "drain the sea" hero shot of the Strait of Gibraltar on real elevation data, as a reusable three.js stage plus a lab page. It is a pure function of time and uses the same window.ready / renderFrame / grabBlob contract as film.html.

**Data and bake**
- Heights: ETOPO 2022 15" (about 450 m, seafloor and land) for an 8x4 degree hero tile, with SRTM-grade detail (Terrarium z10) added on land only. Packed to 4096x2048.
- Horizon skirt: a wide ETOPO 30" tile (-24..12 E, 26..46 N), so there is no visible mesh edge and the Earth curves away into haze.
- Land colour: Blue Marble NG at 500 m, pan-sharpened with luminance from a clear MODIS day at 250 m (2024-08-04, 0.5% cloud over land).
- Light: an offline numpy bake (about 50 s) of soft sun shadows (horizon-angle ray march, about 2 degree penumbra) and 12-direction ambient occlusion at about 200 m.
- Fact check: sill.py flood-fills the data. The Atlantic and Mediterranean disconnect below -287 m, which matches the real Camarinal Sill of about 280-300 m. The page only shows "LAND BRIDGE" when the level is below that, which fixes the false label in the scout prototype.

**Rendering (www/lab/drain/terrain.js, class TerrainStage)**
- Hero mesh 1400x700 plus skirt mesh 720x400, 3x vertical exaggeration, real Earth curvature in the vertex shader.
- Per-pixel normals from a half-float height texture, with offsets scaled to the pixel footprint so distant terrain does not alias.
- Land albedo from the satellite drape. The exposed seabed is procedural sediment (sand shelf, mud slope, silt basin, rock on steep slopes, darker hollows).
- When the water drops: a dark wet band just above the waterline, a white salt crust above that (like Lake Mead's ring), and paler dry crust higher up.
- Water is one curved sheet whose depth is read per pixel from the height maps. It has a turquoise-to-navy colour ramp, see-through shallows, Fresnel sky reflection, slowly drifting wind slicks and a soft shoreline.
- Height-aware aerial haze (exponential layer, warmer toward the sun), an analytic sky with the correct horizon dip, an HDR half-float target with 4x MSAA, and one grade pass (ACES curve, split-tone, vignette, grain).
- Text is drawn on a 2D layer after the grade, so it stays crisp.

**Lab page (www/lab_drain.html)**
- 16 s timeline: sea level 0 m, live drain to -350 m (strait closes, t = 1.5-6.5 s), hold, then down to -1,100 m (t = 8.5-13.5 s), leaving the West Alboran basin as a lake with a salt ring.
- Slow camera push from 32 to 27 km altitude, heading about 68 degrees, pitch about -16 degrees. The horizon sits about 20% from the top of the frame.
- Phone-floor UI: a persistent SEA LEVEL gauge on a navy plate (168 px Bebas number, about 118 px cap height, with a moving level bar) and one 84 px place label at a time, with a leader line.
- Query switches: level, ui, cam, samples, exposure, seaRelief, coast, dbg.

**Before reference (www/lab_drain_before.html)**
- Uses ep01's globe.js copied unchanged, at the same place and heading, at ep01's closest tilted regional camera (alt 0.12, tilt 55) with a 500 m GIBS patch, which is generous to ep01. It uses ep01's 34 px label.

**Measured (audit metric: mean luma, share of near-black pixels)**
- Before: 73/255 and 2.5% near-black.
- After: 119, 142 and 143 for the three levels, all 0% near-black. The benchmark target is 90-140.

**Iterations and self-critique**
- v1 was broken, and three bugs were found and fixed: a sign error in the haze integral, flipped triangle winding that culled every surface, and a debug mode to isolate them.
- v2 was milky, the seabed looked like snow and the sky filled 40% of the frame. Fixed with a lower sun (rebaked), thinner haze, a deeper sky, darker albedos, and a heading/pitch camera.
- v3 fixed the label colliding with the gauge, lifted shadow fill, and added a concavity term, the salt ring, a shading-only seabed relief boost (1.6x), and the -1,100 m drained level so a pool remains.

**Rules followed**
- Nothing was written into lib/, the symlinked asset folders or the production engine.
- Raw downloads (113 MB) were deleted.
- New data is 26 MB under www/lab/drain/data. Outputs are 2.6 MB of JPEGs.

I built a phone-first type and map-graphics system for the engine and used it to redesign three ep01 moments that the audit flagged as unreadable on phones. Each "after" keeps the same information as the ep01 frame, with new graphics and a closer, off-centre camera.

1. Shot A, 0:25, "So are nearly nine in ten of us". Ep01 had a grey 30 px-cap label, a 26 px bar and a globe about 900 px wide in black. The redesign puts a stat block in the left third: the kicker "NEARLY", then a big yellow "9 IN 10" whose digit rolls like an odometer, then a row of 10 people icons (9 filled), then "LIVE NORTH". The globe fills the frame height on the right. The equator is a 9 px line with a dark under-stroke, and the southern hemisphere is darkened in the globe texture. An "EQUATOR" label plate sits on the line it names.

2. Shot B, 3:02, Antarctica opposite the Arctic Ocean. Ep01 had a 7-word caption at 26 px cap, 3 px outlines and a colour legend shown elsewhere. The redesign uses a stacked headline in which the coloured words act as the legend: "ANTARCTICA" in orange, then "IS OPPOSITE THE", then "ARCTIC OCEAN" in cyan. The mirrored Antarctica gets a 66% orange fill with a 5.5 px white outline and glow. The Arctic Ocean is a soft cyan fill with crisp coasts (land is cut out after a blur) and no outline, so the straight sea-boundary lines from ep01 are gone.

3. Shot C, 13:40, "Two: the Pacific closes". Ep01 had thin arrows and no text. The redesign adds a "MODEL [2]" tag with four progress pips (2 of 4), the headline "PACIFIC" (cyan) "CLOSES", and two thick yellow arrows: 15 px body, 63 px head, dark under-stroke and moving highlight dashes so they read as motion. The Pacific gets a cyan tint that stays crisp at coasts and fades out to the south.

4. A style card rendered by the same page, showing every role at its real size with its rules, plus the palette and a crossed-out sample of the old ep01 label.

The size rules are set by cap height at 1080p (the phone player shows it at about 0.203x):
- **Number:** Anton, cap 150-190 px, about 35 px on a phone.
- **Headline:** Anton, cap 96-120 px, about 22 px on a phone.
- **Label:** Barlow Condensed 800 in capitals, cap 64 px (13 px on a phone), always on a plate (86% ink) with an accent bar in the colour of the thing it names.
- **Kicker:** cap 48 px, which is the floor for any text.
- **Text without a plate:** gets a dark stroke of 0.13 x cap height and sits over a side scrim.

Both fonts were already in www/fonts; nothing was downloaded. Colours: orange #FF5A36 for the subject, cyan #3DE3FF for water and "the other side", yellow #FFD23F for numbers, arrows and counted things, #F4F6FA for text. There is no grey text.

- **Pass 2:** fixed people icons that looked like blobs, the EQUATOR label sitting off-frame, and a cropped population area.

API (`import * as T from './lib/type.js'`):
- **Setup:** call `await T.init(H)` once. It measures cap-height ratios: Anton 0.86, Barlow Condensed 0.70, Bebas Neue 0.655.
- **Text:**
  - `T.txt(ctx, s, x, y, {fam, cap, color, stroke:true, align})` draws text sized by cap height (cached sprites).
  - `T.stack(ctx, [{role:'kicker'|'headline'|'label', cap?, words:[{w, c}], lead?}], x, y, lt, {t0, per, tOut})` draws the one text block of a shot; words rise out of a mask, and coloured words replace a legend.
  - `T.label(ctx, s, x, y, {anchor, accent, leader:[x,y], p, t})` draws a label plate with an accent bar and an optional leader line to a pin.
- **Numbers and counts:**
  - `T.slot(ctx, value, x, y, {cap, to, color})` is the odometer number.
  - `T.people(ctx, x, y, n, k, {h, p})` is the "N in 10" icon row.
  - `T.tag(ctx, 'MODEL', i, n, x, y, {p})` is the list tag with pips.
- **Lines and shapes:**
  - `T.projectRuns(globe, rings, {maxLat})` returns visible screen runs; a NaN longitude breaks a run (use it for seam meridians).
  - `T.line(ctx, runs, {width, p, color})` and `T.outline(ctx, runs, {glow})` draw lines and shape outlines.
  - `T.arrow(ctx, pts, {p, width, t})` draws an arrow.
  - `T.pin(ctx, x, y, {t})` draws a map pin.
- **Background:** `T.scrim(ctx, W, H, 'left')` darkens one side behind text; `T.navySpace(ctx, W, H, cx, cy)` lifts black space to navy and leaves the globe and stars alone.
- **QC and constants:** `T.QC.begin()` / `T.QC.report()` give the smallest cap height on the frame and the texts under the 44 px floor. Constants are T.CAP, T.FLOOR, T.C.

3. **Weak north/south contrast (A):** the equator sits low in the frame, so the darkened southern hemisphere is barely visible. Tilt the camera or place the equator at about 65% of frame height.
4. **Antarctica arrow cropped (C):** the Antarctica arrow is partly cut off at the bottom edge. The camera can't show both Brazil and Antarctica large, so it needs a two-shot whip-pan or a dropped arrow.
5. **Hand-placed layout:** each shot's text position and camera offset are set by hand. Scaling needs an auto-layout helper that picks the free third from the subject's projected bounding box. The EQUATOR placement is an ad-hoc search along the line; it needs a general label-on-line placer with collision avoidance between labels.
6. **Missing exits:** only build-in animations exist. T.stack has a tOut exit, but label, tag, slot and people do not.
7. **Word count:** B's headline is 5 words across three lines, one over the audit's 4-word cap.
8. **Untested pairings:** not yet tried with the other builder's cinematic globe (CineGlobe) or on bright daylight terrain shots. On bright frames the side scrim may darken the subject, and a plate behind the headline may be needed instead.
9. **No QC gate:** nothing yet fails a render when a frame breaks the size floor or has more than 2 text blocks. Must-read text also needs a role flag so the 60 px must-read floor can be checked separately from the 44 px floor for any text.

Scaling to a whole film: about 4-6 hours to promote type.js into lib, swap F.pill/F.headline/F.counter in lib/shots.js for T.* equivalents (with the old functions kept as deprecated), add the text layer after post in film.html, and add a QC gate in render.cjs that fails on the [typeqc] FAIL lines and writes a phone sheet of each shot's middle frame with sheet.py. After that every shot inherits the floor automatically. Per-shot work becomes choosing one text block, one hero colour and a camera offset.

result.built:
I built a story mode called "Archive in the World". Real people appear as public-domain photos cut out like paper and placed inside the same photoreal Earth as the rest of the film. They share the globe's light, the same colour grade and the same phone-sized type. There are no low-poly characters, no empty void sets and no static portrait cards.

Two templates are built, one for each ep01 beat:

**A. Bacon, 1620 (replaces the static portrait and Latin plates at 1:00-1:25)**
- Bacon's real 1617 portrait is cut out of its background with a free portrait-matting model (MODNet, run on the CPU), holes in the cut are filled, and it gets a thin paper edge and the shared archival colour tone.
- The cut-out slides in from the left with a slight overshoot. A cool rim light on his edge comes from the globe side, there is a soft drop shadow, a backlight glow separates him from space, and a warm light leak and drifting dust add life.
- He pushes in slowly, faster than the globe behind him, which gives the 2.5D parallax.
- Behind him, the globe fills the frame height. South America and Africa light up in the praised antipode style: semi-transparent orange fill, glow and a crisp white outline. Two thick yellow arrows grow south from Cape Horn and Cape Agulhas.
- The quote is 148 px Bebas, "POINTED TOWARD THE SOUTH.", with SOUTH in orange. The name tag reads "FRANCIS BACON 1620" at 70 px.

**B. Austria said yes (replaces the grey corridor at 7:35-7:50)**
- Wegener's real portrait becomes a paper standee standing on the tilted photoreal Europe, sharpened with a new 500 m NASA GIBS image patch (Blue Marble shaded relief).
- He pops up from flat at Hamburg like a pop-up book, crouches, hops along a dashed yellow arc while the camera follows, and lands on Graz with squash, overshoot and a dust puff.
- The standee has a contact shadow and a cast shadow on the ground. Above the horizon there is a blue sky gradient instead of starry black, and tilt-shift blur at the top and bottom gives a miniature look.
- Austria lights up orange on landing. The headline "AUSTRIA SAID YES." is 158 px with YES in orange, and a "GRAZ 1924" name plate is glued to the base of the standee.

**Measured on the stills**
- Bacon beat: mean brightness 29 before, 50 after (out of 255); near-black share of the frame 56% before, 25% after.
- Corridor beat: mean brightness 32 before, 65 after; near-black share 16% before, 2% after.
- All text is at least 66 px at 1080p, and it reads on the 390 px phone stills.

**Iterations (at least four)**
1. Fixed text clipped at the top, a missing font weight, and the Bacon globe framed so close that Africa was out of shot.
2. Brought both continents into frame and both southern tips into the shot, replaced a dark rectangle with a soft text plate, and moved Bacon lower so the straight crop edge of the painting is off-screen.
3. Wegener: made the standee 0.047 Earth radii tall (fine-tuned to 0.043 in the next pass), about 50% of the frame height. Lowered the hop arc so it no longer crossed the horizon into space. Replaced the starfield with a sky that follows the curve of the horizon, and added the 500 m patch.
4. Moved the Graz plate onto the standee's base (it had been clipped at the frame edge, then floated over the Czech Republic), and added the camera follow during the hop so the Hamburg moment reads.

I also removed matte holes in Bacon's coat and a red strip of painting background above his hat.
result.production_use:
**Files** (all in the sandbox, nothing in the shared lib/ was touched)
- Page: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/visual_lab/engine/www/lab_story.html. It is a copy of film.html with the same window.renderFrame / window.grabBlob contract, and it loads lab/story/edit.js.
- Render: `cd /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/visual_lab/engine && node still.cjs --page lab_story.html --frames 78,270 --outdir OUT`. Scene A runs 0-5 s and scene B 5-12 s. Tuning values can be passed through --q, for example `{"aalt":2,"alo":-0.17,"balt":0.17}`.
- Code: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/visual_lab/engine/www/lab/story/ holds story.js (the library), edit.js (the two scenes), and snapshot copies of globe.js, fx.js and geo.js. The only change to the globe.js copy is its import path.

**Asset pipeline per person** (about 2 minutes each)
1. `python3 -I lab/story/tools/cutout.py modnet.onnx IN.jpg img/NAME` writes NAME_cut.png.
   - The model is MODNet, 25 MB, from https://huggingface.co/Xenova/modnet/resolve/main/onnx/model.onnx, run with onnxruntime on the CPU. I deleted it after use to save disk.
2. `python3 -I lab/story/tools/card.py img/NAME_cut.png img/NAME_card.png --h 900 --edge 9 [--bw] [--tone 0.45] [--close 21]` turns the cut into the paper card. `--close` fills matte holes in dark clothing, and `--bw` applies the full split-tone for black-and-white photos.
3. For sharp close-ups of a region: `python3 -I lab/story/tools/gibs_patch.py LON0 LAT0 LON1 LAT1 img/patch.jpg` fetches a NASA GIBS patch at about 500 m. Install it with `g.setPatch(url, bounds)`.

**story.js API**
- `prepCard(img, {light:'left', rimColor, rimAlpha})` is a one-time step: directional shading, rim light and a soft silhouette for shadows.
- `drawCard(ctx, card, x, yBottom, hPx, {rot, shadowAlpha, shadowDx, shadowDy, alpha})` draws template A, the cut-out in front of the globe.
- `standee(ctx, globe, card, {lat, lon, h (Earth radii), lift, hinge 0..1, squash, lean, shLat, shLon, shAlpha})` draws template B, the standee on the globe, with the pop-up hinge, hop and squash, and contact and cast shadows. It returns `{x, y, top, w, h}` so labels can attach to it.
- Effects:
  - `dust(ctx, t, {seed, n})`
  - `leak(ctx, x, y, r, rgb, a)`
  - `tiltShift(ctx, W, H, {top, bottom})`
  - `sky(ctx, globe, W, H)`: sky gradient that follows the horizon curve
  - `grade(ctx, W, H)`: the shared grade, applied to the world layer before the text
- Text and graphics:
  - `arrow(ctx, pts, p)`: 15 px line, 50 px head
  - `bigLines(ctx, [[{w, c}]], x, y, lt, {size})`
  - `plate(ctx, x, y, w, h)`

**Rules for the whole film**
- Every human beat uses one of the two templates.
  - A, the cut-out in front of the globe: at most 3-4 s, with the person on the left third and the place he talks about lit up on the globe.
  - B, the standee on the map: for moves, events and "he went here" beats. The standee should be at least 40% of frame height and land on the real coordinates.
- Same paper edge, same split-tone, the key light on the same side as the globe's sun, the same grade, and text drawn after the grade.
- One headline of at most 4 words at 140 px or more, plus one name plate of 66 px or more.
- Comedy comes from physical paper motion: pop-up, hop, squash, wobble, a fall-over. Pair it with sound cues (paper flap, whoosh on the hop, a thunk on landing, impact_short).

**Scaling to a film**
- Expect about 10-20 human beats per film, each 3-6 s, so about 1-2 minutes of runtime.
- Each beat needs one cut-out (about 2 minutes of preparation) plus about 30 lines of scene code reusing story.js.
- To merge into production, move story.js into lib/ and add `api.drawStandee` and `api.drawCutout` helpers to film.html.
result.render_cost:
- **Local (software WebGL):** 12 stills across both scenes took 11.7 s, about 1.0 s per frame, of which the globe takes about 0.4 s. Page load with the 5 MB patch and two cards takes about 3 s.
- **Per-frame 2D work:** blits, two radial gradients, a 1/2-1/4-1/8 downscale chain for the tilt-shift, and 16 ray-casts for the horizon. There is no ctx.filter and no shadowBlur. All heavy steps (matting, paper edge, grade, rim, silhouette) are done once per person.
- **Colab L4 GPU:** the extra cost should be negligible (estimated under 10 ms per frame on top of the globe). A 6 s beat is about 180 frames, roughly a few seconds of GPU time.
- **Disk:** source assets total 11.7 MB in lab/story/img: cards 1.2-2.3 MB each, cut PNGs 1.6-2.9 MB, the Central Europe patch 4.0 MB. The output folder research/visual/proto_story is 9.4 MB. The 25 MB model download and all iteration frames were deleted.
result.remaining_work:
**Look**
1. The Bacon frame is still on the dark side: mean brightness 50, against the 70-110 target. The night-side ocean of the globe dominates. Fixes: a brighter "story globe" exposure preset, or tilt the camera so more of the lit hemisphere fills the frame.
2. The cast shadow is a sheared silhouette, not a true projection. It reads as a dark slab under the card's base at some angles. Fixes: a softer and shorter shadow, or a real three.js plane mesh in the globe scene so depth and lighting are correct.
3. In its first ~0.2 s the pop-up hinge shows a flat smear at the horizon. Fixes: start at 30-40 degrees, or start it off-screen.
4. The standee has no thickness or back face, and there is no motion blur on the hop.

**Assets and coverage**
5. MODNet is a portrait-only model. Group or event photos (for example the 1930 Greenland photo) need a general matting model such as BiRefNet (too big for current disk) or hand-drawn masks.
6. The planned third template, a "living photo" (full-bleed 2.5D parallax of an event photo with a clean background plate, dust and a light leak, at most 3 s), is not built. cutout.py already contained a rough background-plate in-painter, but its output had artefacts and was deleted.
7. Bust cut-outs come from cropped portraits, so their bottoms are straight. Full-body figures need full-body PD photos.
8. Terrain outside the GIBS patch is still blocky at low altitude. Only one patch slot is active at a time.

**Production**
9. No sound cues are wired up yet.
10. Fact rule: every standee must land on the real place and year, and the name plates must stay factual. The paper-cut look keeps it obviously a graphic, not fake footage.
11. The other builders' parallel look work (the cinematic globe, the shared LUT) should feed this mode's grade so the whole film shares one look.
